- Check pickups and tonal options. Test each pickup position. If a guitar has coil-splitting/coil-tap, try that — it gives you more tonal variety (useful if you want both thick humbucker tones and single-coil-like sounds).
- Test open D (or any alternate tuning) if that’s important to you. Try an open D setup in the shop or at least simulate lower tunings: heavier-gauge strings and a proper setup are important for good tone and intonation in lower tunings.

- Listen for sustain, resonance, and balance. Pick a note, let it ring, and compare how long and even it sustains across strings.
- Check setup and hardware. Make sure frets are even, tuners hold tune, electronics and pots are clean (no crackling), and intonation is correct.
- Try it through an amp you like. Bring a cable and, if possible, try the guitar through the amp/settings you’d use so you hear the real tone (and test pickup switching and coil-split sounds through the amp).
- Comfort & weight. Les Pauls are typically heavier; make sure it’s comfortable for the length of time you’ll play.
- Consider string gauge and suggested setup. If you plan to use open D, consider a heavier string set and ask about a setup optimized for that tuning.
